topComments.author: zbentley
topComments.text: EventQL seems nice, but > While an EventQL precondition is evaluated, every other write waits, so that nothing can come in between; reads go on meanwhile. So that no write holds up the others for long, the EventQL preconditions of a write are evaluated for at most five seconds, all of them together, counted from when the write gets its turn: a write whose preconditions take longer is rejected, with nothing written, with a 400 (From https://www.eventfoundation.io/docs/eventsourcingdb/precondi... ) That seems like a huge foot gun. Like, sure, you don't have to implement transactional semantics or think about consistency/MVCC/snapshots. But at the cost of "every UPDATE ... WHERE prevents every other write for up to 5 seconds"? Really? That seems like a bad tradeoff, inferior to both (massive effort) implementing proper transactionality, (medium efffort, but significantly compatibility-breaking) removing support for hierarchically-nested subjects so that the global-mutex restrictions on UPDATE-WHERE can be lifted/efficiently scoped to a subject, or (lowest effort) removing support for EventQL preconditions entirely. In any sufficiently large/multi-developer system I don't imagine that "don't use EventQL preconditions" will effectively stick. As it is, I feel like having the main event sourcing system blocked for up to 5sec on any one client's slow EventQL precondition is asking for pervasive downtime events out of nowhere. That said, I may be missing something that ameliorates those issues! I'm just skimming docs, so take it with a grain of salt.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: How can I exclude sampling gaps when calculating accompanying time between two Ganos trajectories?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am using Ganos in PolarDB for PostgreSQL to calculate how long two trajectories remain within a specified distance of each other. I need to exclude missing-data intervals. My rule is: Linearly interpolate between consecutive samples only when their time difference is 120 seconds or less . If the time difference exceeds 120 seconds, treat the interval between those samples as unknown. Count accompanying time only when both trajectories have valid positions. Do not merge accompanying intervals across unknown periods. The following synthetic example uses Cartesian coordinates and a distance threshold of 2 coordinate units . Sample data and current query Trajectory A has a sampling gap between seconds 120 and 480. Trajectory B has a different gap, between seconds 60 and 420. WITH samples(track_id, seconds, x, y) AS ( VALUES ('A', 0, 0.0, 0.0), ('A', 60, 1.0, 0.0), ('A', 120, 2.0, 0.0), ('A', 480, 8.0, 0.0), ('A', 540, 9.0, 0.0), ('A', 600, 10.0, 0.0), ('B', 0, 0.0, 1.0), ('B', 60, 1.0, 1.0), ('B', 420, 7.0, 1.0), ('B', 480, 8.0, 1.0), ('B', 540, 9.0, 1.0), ('B', 600, 10.0, 1.0) ), tracks AS ( SELECT track_id, ST_MakeTrajectory( 'STPOINT'::leaftype, ST_MakeLine( ST_MakePoint( x::double precision, y::double precision ) ORDER BY seconds ), array_agg( timestamp '2026-01-01 00:00:00' + seconds * interval '1 second' ORDER BY seconds ), NULL ) AS traj FROM samples GROUP BY track_id ) SELECT result.start_time, result.end_time, EXTRACT( EPOCH FROM result.end_time - result.start_time ) AS duration_seconds FROM tracks AS a CROSS JOIN tracks AS b CROSS JOIN LATERAL ST_AccompanyIntervals( a.traj, b.traj, 2.0::double precision, interval '0 seconds', interval '0 seconds', 'C'::character(1) ) AS result WHERE a.track_id = 'A' AND b.track_id = 'B' ORDER BY result.start_time; The 'C' argument selects coordinate-based distance calculation. stackOverflowQuestions.title: Do you compare raw output values or only the final prediction when validating a deployed model?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I'm deploying a small classification model on an NXP-based embedded target and I'm currently setting up some verification tests. One thing I'm unsure about is what I should actually compare. The raw output values from the deployed model are never exactly the same as the TensorFlow model, especially after quantization. For example: Python: TensorFlow: [0.72, 0.18, 0.10] C: Embedded: [0.68, 0.22, 0.10] Both models predict the same class, but the scores differ. In practice, do you compare the actual output values with a tolerance, or do you only care that the final prediction remains unchanged?

infoqArticles.title: GitHub Makes Agentic Workflows Generally Available with Isolation and Budget Controls
infoqArticles.description: GitHub Agentic Workflows is generally available, running coding agents in GitHub Actions with read-only defaults and separately scoped write jobs. infoqArticles.author: Mark Silvester

infoqArticles.title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
infoqArticles.description: JioHotstar evaluated 6 approaches to code retrieval for AI coding agents using SWE, CodeScale Bench, and an internal question-answering harness. Structural search performed well on concrete tasks, while semantic retrieval helped with ambiguous requirements. The findings highlight trade-offs in accuracy, token use, and tool design, underscoring the need to match retrieval tools to task types. By Le
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: How LinkedIn, Netflix & DoorDash Run Agents, Evals & Inference in Production: QCon AI New York 2026
infoqArticles.description: QCon AI New York has published its full program for December 15–16, 2026. Engineers from LinkedIn, Netflix, DoorDash, Figma, Pinterest, Honeycomb, Harvey, Google DeepMind and OpenAI describe AI systems they run in production. Talks cover agent permissions and guardrails, eval loops, inference cost, AI code review, and team adoption. By Artenisa Chatziou
infoqArticles.author: Artenisa Chatziou

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Uncorking Queueing Bottlenecks with OpenTelemetry
infoqArticles.description: Oli Lane and Julian Wreford share how Gearset replaced guesswork in distributed asynchronous queues with OpenTelemetry tracing. They explain why traditional metrics fall short, how to implement user-centric SLOs based on latency distributions, and share practical debugging tips to help senior developers, software architects, and engineering leaders improve system reliability and team culture. By J
infoqArticles.author: Julian Wreford, Oli Lane

infoqArticles.title: Article: The iOS Crash We Could Not Reproduce
infoqArticles.description: This article describes the investigation to find the root cause of a production crash in a large-scale iOS consumer app that had no clean stack trace. The crash occurred intermittently and resisted every local reproduction attempt. The final code change was small, but identifying the root cause required turning a vague SIGBUS report into a controlled set of experiments. By Abhishek Gang Deb
infoqArticles.author: Abhishek Gang Deb

infoqArticles.title: Angular's TypeScript 7-Powered Compiler Enters Beta with Rust-Based Preprocessor
infoqArticles.description: The Angular team has introduced ngp, a compiler preprocessor that rewrites the analysis stage in Rust using Oxc. It replaces ngc's dependence on the Transformer API, which TypeScript 7.0 removed. An early benchmark showed 2x to 3x faster cold builds. Adoption is expected in an Angular 22 minor release; production builds should stay on ngc until then. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Cloudflare Makes Basin Serverless Analytics Generally Available
infoqArticles.description: Cloudflare has announced the general availability of Basin, a serverless analytics platform built on Apache Iceberg and R2 Object Storage. The managed service supports open data formats and integrates with tools such as DuckDB, Snowflake, and Apache Spark, with no data egress fees. By Renato Losio
infoqArticles.author: Renato Losio

infoqArticles.title: Google Finds that Technical Debt Can Derail Coding Agents Through "Agent Distraction"
infoqArticles.description: In a recent article, Google senior staff software engineer Sam Saccone and senior staff data scientist Madhuri Garikapati highlighted the cost of agent distraction, where AI coding agents get derailed by stale technical debt, such as old TODO comments, obsolete bug references, and outdated specs, leading them to embark on unrequested "side-quests". By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Pinterest and Intel Take Open-Source Profiling to Internet Scale

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Batch Intelligence at Scale: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience
infoqArticles.description: Aditya Mulik explains how Walmart Global Tech deployed multi-agent LLM workflows across 4,700 stores for nightly batch inventory forecasting. He discusses tackling production hurdles - schema violations, cross-department data mismatches, and network drops - via MCP grounding and loop agents, while slashing cloud inference costs from $100k+ to $10k per month shifting from PTUs to pay-as-you-go. By
infoqArticles.author: Aditya Mulik

infoqArticles.title: Article: LLM Reliability Layers Under Test: Accuracy, Yield, and the Limits of Verification
infoqArticles.description: Verification layers sort outputs by trust rather than fixing errors. In a benchmark of six reliability layers, voting and self-correction failed to recover accuracy - they only withheld doubtful records. Production systems gain more reliability by replacing generation with deterministic lookups, tracking yield over raw accuracy, and resolving extraction bottlenecks before stacking checks. By Pushp
infoqArticles.author: Pushpdeep Mishra, Wejdan Bagais

infoqArticles.title: Google Cloud Spend Caps Reach General Availability with API and Monthly Resets

GA adds an API, estimated live costs, and automatic monthly resets, but caps cover only the Gemini API, the Agent Platform, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions, and overages during enforcement delays are still billed. infoqArticles.title: Effect 4.0 Ships: Dependency-Free Rewrite with 5x Smaller Bundles and Long-Term Support
